questions.stem: Why does air heated strongly at the ground tend to produce an area of low pressure at the surface?
options: Warm air expands, becomes less dense and rises, so less air presses on the surface
Warm air contracts, becomes more dense and sinks, so more air presses on the surface
Warm air absorbs all of the water vapour, so it weighs nothing at the surface
Warm air moves towards the poles, leaving no air at all above the ground
questions.explanation: Heated air expands and rises, so the weight of air above the surface is reduced, giving low pressure. Cooling makes air contract and sink, building high pressure. Rising air also cools and forms cloud, which is why lows often bring rain.

questions.stem: Wind at Earth's surface blows from:
options: The poles towards the equator in every location
Areas of high pressure towards areas of low pressure
Areas of low pressure towards areas of high pressure
Cold areas towards warm areas regardless of pressure
questions.explanation: Air moves down the pressure gradient, from high to low pressure. Its path is then deflected by Earth's rotation, so it does not flow straight across the isobars.

questions.stem: Air rises near the equator, flows towards the poles at high altitude, sinks around 30° latitude and returns towards the equator at the surface. What is this circulation called, and what surface winds does it produce?
options: A Ferrel cell, producing the polar easterlies
A Hadley cell, producing the trade winds
A polar cell, producing the westerlies
A Walker cell, producing the monsoon
questions.explanation: The Hadley cell is driven by strong heating near the equator. Air sinking near 30° forms the subtropical high-pressure belt, and air returning towards the equator at the surface, deflected by Earth's rotation, forms the trade winds.

questions.stem: Much of inland Australia lies near 25 to 30° S and is arid. How does systematic atmospheric circulation help explain this?
options: Moist air rises in the subtropical low-pressure belt, cooling and producing heavy rain
Cold polar air flows over the region all year, so water vapour freezes before rain forms
Westerly winds bring moist ocean air over the region all year, but it never condenses
Dry air sinks in the subtropical high-pressure belt, warming and suppressing cloud and rain
questions.explanation: Air that rose and lost its moisture near the equator sinks around 30° latitude. Sinking air warms and dries, which suppresses cloud formation, so the subtropics contain many of the world's deserts, including much of inland Australia.

questions.stem: In the Southern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air:
options: Directly towards the nearest pole only
To the left of its direction of motion
To the right of its direction of motion
Straight upwards away from the surface
questions.explanation: Earth's rotation deflects moving air and water to the left in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. This is why winds circulate clockwise around lows and anticlockwise around highs in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.stem: Above the friction of the surface, wind blows almost parallel to the isobars rather than straight from high to low pressure. What is this wind called, and why does it flow this way?
options: Geostrophic wind, because the pressure gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis effect
Trade wind, because air sinking in the subtropics is pushed directly towards the equator
Sea breeze, because land heats faster than water and draws air in from the coast
Jet stream, because friction with mountains turns the wind until it runs along them
questions.explanation: Air starts moving towards low pressure, but the Coriolis effect deflects it until the two forces balance, leaving the wind flowing parallel to the isobars. Near the ground, friction slows the wind and weakens the deflection, so surface winds cross the isobars at an angle.

questions.stem: How does systematic atmospheric circulation affect Earth's energy distribution?
options: It transfers thermal energy from the tropics, which have a surplus, towards the poles
It transfers thermal energy from the poles, which have a surplus, towards the tropics
It keeps all thermal energy at the latitude where the sunlight was first absorbed
It transfers thermal energy from the surface to the core through convection
questions.explanation: Low latitudes receive more solar energy than they emit, and high latitudes emit more than they receive. Air circulation, together with ocean currents, carries heat and latent heat poleward, preventing the tropics from heating and the poles from cooling without limit.

questions.stem: The Walker Circulation is an east-west loop of air over the tropical Pacific Ocean. In normal conditions, where does air rise and where does it sink?
options: It rises over the warm western Pacific near Indonesia and sinks over the cooler eastern Pacific
It rises over the cool eastern Pacific near South America and sinks over the western Pacific
It rises over Antarctica and sinks over the equator, driving the westerly winds
It rises over Australia's interior deserts and sinks over the warm Coral Sea
questions.explanation: Warm water in the western Pacific heats the air, which rises, forming cloud and rain over Indonesia and northern Australia. Air flows east aloft, sinks over the cooler eastern Pacific and returns west at the surface as the easterly trade winds.

questions.stem: On a synoptic chart, isobars are lines joining places of equal:
options: Temperature
Rainfall
Humidity
Air pressure
questions.explanation: Isobars join places with the same mean sea-level air pressure, usually labelled in hectopascals (hPa). Lines of equal temperature are isotherms.

questions.stem: On a synoptic chart, isobars are packed closely together over Bass Strait but widely spaced over central Queensland. What can be concluded?
options: Rain is falling over Bass Strait, because isobars always mark rain bands
Temperatures are higher over Bass Strait, because isobars join warm places
Winds are stronger over Bass Strait, because the pressure gradient is steeper there
Winds are stronger over central Queensland, because the isobars are further apart
questions.explanation: The closer the isobars, the faster pressure changes over distance, so the pressure gradient and wind speed are greater. Widely spaced isobars indicate light winds. Isobars show pressure, not rainfall or temperature.

questions.stem: In the Southern Hemisphere, how do winds circulate around a high-pressure system?
options: Anticlockwise and inward towards the centre
Clockwise and outward from the centre
Anticlockwise and outward from the centre
Clockwise and inward towards the centre
questions.explanation: Air flows outward from a high, and the Coriolis effect deflects it to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, producing an anticlockwise circulation. Around a low, air spirals inward and clockwise.

questions.stem: On a synoptic chart, a line with solid triangles moving north-east across Victoria represents:
options: A cold front, where cooler air is replacing warmer air
A warm front, where warmer air is replacing cooler air
A high-pressure ridge, bringing clear and settled weather
A trough of low pressure that brings no change in air mass
questions.explanation: Triangles on a front mark a cold front, pointing in the direction it is moving. Cold fronts bring a change to cooler air, often with a wind change, cloud and showers. Warm fronts are shown with semicircles.

questions.stem: A satellite image shows a large spiral of cloud over the Coral Sea with a clear central eye, and the synoptic chart shows tightly packed, roughly circular isobars around a central pressure of 960 hPa. What does this indicate?
options: A tropical cyclone with very strong winds around a deep low
A high-pressure system bringing clear, calm and dry weather
A cold front bringing a mild change to a cooler southerly
A weak trough with light winds and scattered showers
questions.explanation: A cloud spiral with an eye, very low central pressure and closely spaced isobars indicate a tropical cyclone with destructive winds. High-pressure systems have high central pressures and widely spaced isobars and usually bring clear skies.

questions.stem: Why does meteorology depend on international conventions, such as standard units and symbols on weather charts?
options: Weather systems cross borders, so countries must share and read each other's data accurately
Each country must use different symbols so that its forecasts cannot be copied
International conventions are needed only for climate, not daily weather forecasts
Standard symbols make forecasts more interesting for television audiences
questions.explanation: Weather moves across national boundaries and oceans, so forecasters rely on observations shared worldwide in standard formats. Clear communication supports warnings for aviation, shipping, agriculture and the public.

questions.stem: How do temperature and salinity affect the density of seawater?
options: Warmer and saltier water is denser
Colder and fresher water is denser
Warmer and fresher water is denser
Colder and saltier water is denser
questions.explanation: Cooling makes water contract, increasing its density, and dissolved salt adds mass. So cold, salty water is the densest and sinks below warmer or fresher water.

questions.stem: When sea ice forms around Antarctica, the surrounding seawater becomes saltier. Why does this help drive the ocean conveyor?
options: Salt is left behind as ice freezes, so the very cold, salty water becomes dense and sinks
Sea ice releases heat as it forms, so the surrounding water becomes warmer and rises
Salt in the sea ice melts the ice again, so fresh water flows north and sinks
Sea ice reflects sunlight, which heats the deep ocean and pushes water upward
questions.explanation: Ice is mostly fresh water, so freezing leaves extra salt in the surrounding water. Combined with very low temperatures, this produces some of the densest water in the ocean, which sinks and spreads along the sea floor as part of the conveyor.

questions.stem: In which regions does dense water sink to form the deep part of the global ocean conveyor?
options: The equatorial Pacific and Indian Oceans
The Coral Sea and the Great Barrier Reef
The Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea only
The North Atlantic and around Antarctica
questions.explanation: Deep water forms where surface water becomes very cold and salty: in the North Atlantic and in seas around Antarctica. It then spreads through the deep ocean basins before slowly upwelling elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which list describes the key features of the ocean conveyor in order?
options: Warm water sinks at the equator, rises at the poles and returns through the atmosphere as rain
Surface water spreads from Antarctica, sinks in the tropics and stays permanently on the sea floor
Deep water rises at the poles, cools at the equator and returns as icebergs to the North Atlantic
Dense water sinks, spreads through the deep ocean, upwells broadly and returns in near-surface currents
questions.explanation: Water sinks in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica, spreads slowly through the deep ocean, rises gradually over wide areas and returns through near-surface currents such as the Gulf Stream. A complete loop takes many hundreds of years.

questions.stem: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the tropics north-east across the Atlantic. How does it affect north-western Europe?
options: It transfers cold water that makes summers cooler than at similar latitudes
It removes all moisture from the air, so north-western Europe has little rainfall
It has the same effect as the cold currents that flow along western coasts
It transfers heat that makes winters milder than at similar latitudes elsewhere
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream and its extension carry tropical heat poleward, releasing it to the atmosphere and making winters in north-western Europe milder than in places at similar latitudes such as eastern Canada. It is a warm current, not a cold one.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why surface currents in the open ocean, such as the large gyres, move in broad circular patterns?
options: Prevailing winds drag the surface water, and Earth's rotation deflects it
Differences in salinity alone push surface water from the poles to the equator
Heat from the sea floor drives water upward and outward in circles
Tides pull the surface water around each ocean basin once a day
questions.explanation: Surface currents are driven mainly by winds such as the trade winds and westerlies, and the Coriolis effect deflects the moving water, so currents form large rotating gyres. Density differences mainly drive the deep circulation.

questions.stem: The East Australian Current flows south along Queensland's and New South Wales's coasts. What type of current is it?
options: A cold current carrying Antarctic water towards the equator
A deep current carrying dense water along the sea floor
A tidal current that reverses direction twice each day
A warm current carrying tropical water towards higher latitudes
questions.explanation: The East Australian Current is the western boundary current of the South Pacific gyre, carrying warm tropical water south along the east coast. It influences coastal climate and carries tropical marine species south.

questions.stem: A student puts cold, salty, blue-dyed water gently into one end of a tank of warm fresh water. The blue water sinks and flows along the bottom. Which feature of the ocean conveyor does this model, and what is one limitation?
options: The upwelling of deep water; it ignores the effect of temperature on density
The Gulf Stream; it ignores the fact that warm water is denser than cold water
Wind-driven gyres; it ignores the effect of salinity on surface currents
The sinking and spreading of dense deep water; it ignores Earth's rotation and wind
questions.explanation: The model shows dense, cold and salty water sinking and flowing along the bottom, as deep water does in the conveyor. It leaves out Earth's rotation, wind, basin shapes and the slow timescales of the real ocean. Warm water is less dense, not more.

questions.stem: The global oceans have absorbed more than 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases in recent decades. What property allows the oceans to act as such a large heat sink?
options: Water's low density, so warm water quickly sinks and stores heat at depth
Water's high specific heat capacity, combined with the huge volume of the oceans
Water's low specific heat capacity, so it heats up very quickly at the surface
Water's high albedo, which reflects heat downward into the deep ocean
questions.explanation: Water needs a great deal of energy to change temperature, and the oceans hold an enormous mass of water, so they can absorb vast amounts of heat with only small temperature changes. Warm water is less dense and stays near the surface, mixing downward only slowly.

questions.stem: Weather can be described as an interaction between the atmosphere and the hydrosphere. Which example shows this?
options: Lava flowing into the sea and cooling into a new rock platform
Mangrove roots trapping mud along a sheltered estuary bank
Granite slowly weathering to sand in a mountain stream bed
Water evaporating from a warm sea and condensing into storm clouds
questions.explanation: Weather involves exchanges of water and energy between air and water: evaporation from the sea supplies moisture and energy, and condensation produces cloud and rain. The other examples involve the geosphere or biosphere.

questions.stem: During an El Niño event, which changes occur in the tropical Pacific?
options: Trade winds reverse to blow towards Australia from South America
Trade winds stay the same, but the sea near Australia becomes warmer
Trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east, away from Australia
Trade winds strengthen and warm water builds up near Australia
questions.explanation: In El Niño, the trade winds weaken and the warm pool of water shifts towards the central and eastern Pacific. Rising air and rainfall shift east with it, so eastern Australia is often drier than normal. Stronger trades and warm water near Australia describe La Niña.

questions.stem: Which effects on eastern Australia are typical of La Niña?
options: Below-average rainfall, but more frequent snow on the Queensland coast
Above-average temperatures by day and fewer clouds across the east
Above-average rainfall, increased flood risk and more tropical cyclones
Below-average rainfall, drought, and fewer tropical cyclones than usual
questions.explanation: During La Niña, warmer waters near Australia and stronger trade winds increase moisture and rising air, so eastern Australia often has wetter conditions, more flooding and more tropical cyclones. Drought and reduced rainfall are associated with El Niño.

questions.stem: The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) is calculated from differences in air pressure between which two places?
options: Tahiti and Darwin
Perth and Sydney
Hobart and Cairns
Fiji and Jakarta
questions.explanation: The SOI is based on the difference in mean sea-level pressure between Tahiti in the central Pacific and Darwin in northern Australia. It measures the strength of the Walker Circulation.

questions.stem: The Bureau of Meteorology notes that sustained SOI values below −7 often indicate El Niño, and sustained values above +7 often indicate La Niña. The three-month average SOI is +12. Which conditions are most likely?
options: Neutral conditions, because only values above +20 indicate any change
El Niño, because positive values mean higher pressure at Darwin
La Niña, with stronger trade winds and wetter conditions in eastern Australia
El Niño, with weaker trade winds and drier conditions in eastern Australia
questions.explanation: A sustained SOI above +7 is typical of La Niña, which brings stronger trade winds and a wetter east. Positive values mean pressure at Tahiti is relatively high compared with Darwin, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Data for one year show: sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific 1.5 °C above average, a three-month SOI of −14, and below-average winter-spring rainfall in Queensland. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: A positive SAM event, with westerly winds pulled north over Queensland in winter
A neutral year, because sea temperature changes of 1.5 °C are too small to matter
An El Niño event, with warm water shifted east and rising air moving away from Australia
A La Niña event, with cool water shifted east and rising air moving towards Australia
questions.explanation: Warm sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific, a sustained strongly negative SOI and a dry Queensland all fit El Niño. La Niña would show cool eastern Pacific waters, a positive SOI and wetter conditions.

questions.stem: El Niño affects places well beyond Australia. Which global effect is commonly associated with El Niño?
options: Stronger trade winds across the whole Pacific
Heavier rainfall along the normally dry coast of Peru
Heavier monsoon rainfall over Indonesia
Cooler sea temperatures off the coast of Peru
questions.explanation: When warm water and rising air shift east during El Niño, the usually arid coast of Peru can receive heavy rain and warmer seas, while Indonesia and eastern Australia tend to be drier. Stronger trade winds are a La Niña feature.

questions.stem: What is the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)?
options: A belt of westerly winds that moves north and south around Antarctica
A pulse of cloud and rain that moves east along the equator every few weeks
A difference in sea surface temperatures between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean
A difference in air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin in the tropical Pacific Ocean
questions.explanation: The IOD compares sea surface temperatures in the western and eastern parts of the tropical Indian Ocean. The Tahiti-Darwin pressure difference is the SOI, the westerly belt describes the SAM, and the eastward-moving pulse is the Madden-Julian Oscillation.

questions.stem: During a positive Indian Ocean Dipole, waters off Indonesia and north-west Australia are cooler than usual. What is the typical effect on Australian rainfall?
options: Below-average winter and spring rainfall over much of southern and central Australia
Above-average winter and spring rainfall over much of southern and central Australia
Above-average summer monsoon rainfall over northern Australia every year
No change in rainfall anywhere, because the Indian Ocean does not affect Australia
questions.explanation: Cooler water to Australia's north-west means less moisture flows across the continent, so a positive IOD usually brings below-average winter and spring rainfall to southern and central Australia. A negative IOD tends to bring the opposite.

questions.stem: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is best described as:
options: A permanent warm current flowing south along Australia's east coast all year
A change in the sea surface temperature of the Indian Ocean every winter
An eastward-moving pulse of cloud and rainfall near the equator that recurs every 30 to 60 days
A westward-moving belt of high pressure over Antarctica that recurs every 2 to 7 years
questions.explanation: The MJO is a large-scale pulse of enhanced and suppressed cloud and rainfall that travels east around the tropics, typically recurring every 30 to 60 days. It can affect the timing of the northern Australian monsoon and tropical cyclone activity.

questions.stem: In winter, a positive Southern Annular Mode (SAM) shifts the belt of westerly winds and cold fronts closer to Antarctica. What is the likely effect on rainfall in southern Australia, and why?
options: Less rainfall, because fewer cold fronts and storms reach southern Australia
More rainfall, because the westerly winds bring more cold fronts over the south
More rainfall, because the shift brings tropical moisture into southern Victoria
Less rainfall, because the westerly winds move north over central Queensland
questions.explanation: In a positive SAM, the westerlies contract southward, so the cold fronts that bring winter rain more often miss southern Australia, reducing rainfall there. A negative SAM moves the westerlies north, bringing more fronts and rain to the south in winter.

questions.stem: A farmer on the Darling Downs is told that a La Niña is developing and the IOD is forecast to be negative. Which seasonal outlook is most likely?
options: Wetter in the west only, because the Indian Ocean affects only Western Australia
Unchanged, because the effects of the two drivers always cancel each other out
Wetter than average, because both drivers tend to increase rainfall over much of eastern Australia
Drier than average, because both drivers tend to reduce rainfall over eastern Australia
questions.explanation: La Niña tends to bring above-average rainfall to eastern Australia, and a negative IOD tends to increase winter-spring rainfall over much of southern and eastern Australia. When both occur together, the chance of a wet season is increased.

questions.stem: Why is accurate forecasting of El Niño and La Niña important for Queensland?
options: It helps farmers, water managers and emergency services prepare for drought or flood
It allows scientists to stop El Niño events from developing in the Pacific Ocean
It is needed only for tourism, so that visitors can plan their beach holidays
It determines the exact day each cyclone will cross the coast months in advance
questions.explanation: Knowing the likely state of ENSO months ahead allows planting decisions, water storage management and preparation for floods or fires. Forecasts cannot prevent events and give probabilities for seasons rather than the timing of individual storms.
